BREAKING: The 4-week average of US new home listings rose +2.1% in the week ending August 30th, to 383,795, its highest since August 2022.

This exceeds this year’s previous peak of 383,712, set in April.

The increase was led by San Jose, Boston, and Nashville, where listings surged +29.4%, +26.1%, and +21.5%, respectively.

At the same time, the total number of homes for sale rose +0.4% to 1,511,313.

Meanwhile, pending home sales declined -0.1% over the same period to 308,282, the lowest since February, suggesting demand is failing to keep up with rising supply.

This comes as the median sale price rose +2.2% YoY to $398,632, while the average 30Y mortgage rate stood at 6.66%, near its highest over the last 12 months.

Housing market affordability is at record lows.

items.title: Russian gold flows into Hong Kong are skyrocketing: In the first 7 months of 2026, Hong Kong’s gold imports from Russia rose to $14.4 billion. This is already +50% above the full-year figure of $9.6 billion recorded in 2025. This is also nearly triple the amount seen in 2023 and 2024. The surge reflects the redirection of Russian gold exports toward Asian markets after Western sanctions effectively closed London and other Western hubs to Russian bullion. Hong Kong has no such restrictions, allowing it to increasingly serve as a major trading hub for Russian gold entering the Asian market. The flow of Russian gold into Asia is accelerating.

items.content:
The de-dollarization trend appears to be far from global:

The US Dollar’s proportion of official global FX reserves is down to 57%, its lowest in at least 30 years.

This percentage has declined -20 points since 1999, with China and, to a lesser extent, Russia driving much of the decline.

Over the same period, the combined proportion of the 4 major reserve currencies, the US Dollar, Yen, Euro and Pound, has fallen -12 percentage points, to ~87%, also its lowest in at least 30 years.

Meanwhile, roughly equal numbers of countries increased and decreased their US Dollar reserves between 2015 and 2023.

Therefore, the decline is heavily concentrated among a small number of reserve holders, suggesting the US Dollar's position in most reserve portfolios remains relatively stable.

The threat to the US Dollar’s reserve currency status appears limited.
— The Kobeissi Letter (@KobeissiLetter) Sep 7, 2026

items.title: What is happening with the US job market? US job openings for June were revised down by -177,000 vacancies, their largest monthly downward revision since November 2025. This also marks the 3rd consecutive monthly downward revision. Furthermore, the number of hires for June was revised down by -16,000, while the number of quits was revised lower by -19,000. At the same time, the number of layoffs and discharges was revised up by +19,000. As a result, job openings have now been revised down in 38 of the last 43 months. US labor market data is becoming increasingly difficult to read with confidence.

The AI buildout is one of the largest capital spending cycles in history.

items.title: Foreign investors are piling into US assets: Investors outside the US now hold a record ~$39 trillion in US equities, Treasuries, corporate, agency, and other bonds. Since the 2022 bear market, this figure has surged +$16 trillion, or +70%. Over this period, foreign holdings of US stocks have doubled to a record $24 trillion, accounting for ~62% of the total. At the same time, foreign Treasury holdings have grown +$2 trillion, to $8 trillion, an all-time high, representing ~21% of the total. To put this into perspective, during the 2020 pandemic, investors outside the US held just ~$19 trillion in US assets. Foreign demand for US assets is historically strong.

Utilities stocks are at their most oversold levels in years:

Only ~25% of the S&P 500 utility sector stocks are now trading above their 200-day moving average, the lowest proportion since February 2024.

This marks a sharp reversal from ~90% recorded in July.

Utilities have gone from one of the market’s strongest groups, after gaining +11.5% through February, to one of its weakest, with the sector now up only +2.3% year-to-date, putting it on track for its worst year relative to the S&P 500 since 2023.

Investor demand for defensive stocks is fading.

items.content:
Investors are taking on more currency risk:

The exposure-weighted average currency hedge ratio across 6 major markets, including Japan, Canada, and Taiwan, is down to just 41%, the lowest since at least 2015.

This ratio measures the extent to which investors hedge against currency movements, meaning ~59% of their exposure was left unhedged.

This is happening even as hedging becomes cheaper, with 3-month US Dollar hedge costs for Yen-based investors falling to a 4-year low of 2.75%, from as high as 6.00% in October 2023, while costs for Euro-based investors declined to a 2-year low of 1.32%.

Investors have reduced their hedges as the US Dollar historically tends to remain resilient during periods of market volatility.

However, the case for staying unhedged is starting to weaken, as hedging becomes cheaper while the Dollar’s safe-haven appeal comes under pressure and concerns over currency debasement grow.

As a result, these investors, who collectively hold trillions in US assets, have little protection against a weaker US Dollar if the current trend continues.

Investors are increasingly exposed to US Dollar weakness.
— The Kobeissi Letter (@KobeissiLetter) Sep 6, 2026
